498.title: They walk humbly
498.hook: servants of the Merciful walk gently, and when the ignorant address them, say peace (25:63)
498.howItsDone: Muslim teachers often read 25:63–77, the portrait of 'ibad ar-Rahman, as a description of good character, and quote verse 63 when teaching how to respond to insults.

segments.voice: Yesterday, furqan, the criterion, and your line was tell right from wrong. What decision did you finally make? Day four hundred ninety-eight.

Someone cuts in front of you in line and then glares at you as if you'd done it. A stranger online replies to a harmless comment with something cruel. A driver leans on the horn and shouts a word you won't repeat. There's a split second where the body gets ready to answer in kind. Near its end, Surah Al-Furqan paints a portrait of a certain kind of person, and the first two strokes of the portrait are about exactly this: how they walk, and what they say when someone is rude to them.

Verse sixty-three. The portrait has a title: 'ibad ar-Rahman, the servants of the Most Merciful. Pickthall calls them the faithful slaves of the Beneficent, "who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace". Walk modestly is yamshuna hawnan. Hawn means ease, lightness, gentleness. Not slinking, not timid. Just walking without swagger, without needing the street to notice you. Then the foolish ones, al-jahilun. Scholars of early Arabic point out that jahl isn't only not knowing things. It's the opposite of hilm, forbearance. A jahil is someone hot-tempered, rash, quick to insult. So the scene is: someone flares up at them. And they answer, salaman. Peace. Commentators read that in more than one way. Some say it means a word of peace, a calm reply that refuses to escalate. Others say it means they speak in a way that keeps them safe from sin: they say something decent and move on. Neither reading makes it weakness. A hadith in Bukhari says the strong person isn't the one who wins at wrestling; the strong one is the one who controls himself when angry. That's the strength in this verse. The portrait runs on to the end of the surah, and we'll walk through more of it. But it begins here, at street level. How you carry your body down the road. And the first thing you say when someone throws something at you. The servants of the Merciful get their name from Him. The gentleness is borrowed.
screen: `'IBAD AR-RAHMAN.` · `HAWN: EASE, GENTLENESS.` · `JAHL: THE OPPOSITE OF FORBEARANCE.` · `THE STRONG ONE CONTROLS ANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse answering rudeness with peace. Sit, and let the breath settle. Remember the last time someone was short with you. Feel how your body got ready to reply. Now replay it, slowly, and let your shoulders drop instead. Picture yourself saying something calm and short. Peace. Okay. Have a good day. Then walking on, lightly. If you pray, you can ask for that ease. The bell holds the time.
Hawnan. Gently, with ease: how the servants of the Merciful walk the earth, and answer the rash with peace. Today's word.
Your line: walk gently; say peace. Today, the next time someone is rude to you, in person or online, try one calm short reply, or none, and walk on. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

499.title: Between the two
499.hook: when they spend, neither wasteful nor stingy, but in between (25:67)
499.howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite 25:67 and 17:29 on balanced spending, and Islamic law generally limits bequests to one third of an estate, following the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hawnan, they walk humbly, and your line was to walk gently and say peace. Did someone test it? What did you say? Day four hundred ninety-nine.

There are two kinds of people who are hard to go shopping with. One buys everything, the second pair of shoes, the upgrade, the thing that was on sale, and checks the bank balance with one eye closed. The other won't buy a sandwich, counts every coin twice, and somehow makes everyone around them feel guilty for eating. Some people manage to be both in the same week. The portrait of the servants of the Merciful continues, and one of its strokes is about money.
screen: `THE ONE WHO WON'T BUY A SANDWICH.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty-seven. Pickthall: "And those who, when they spend, are neither prodigal nor grudging; and there is ever a firm station between the two". Prodigal is israf, going past the limit, spending beyond what's needed or right. Grudging is qatr, tightening, squeezing, holding back what ought to be given. And between them, qawam. Pickthall calls it a firm station. It's from the same root as standing upright, qama. Qawam is the place where something stands steady, balanced, not tipping either way. So the middle here isn't lukewarm. It's upright. Another surah gives the same picture with a body: don't keep your hand chained to your neck, and don't stretch it out all the way either. And there's a moment in Bukhari that shows what the middle looks like in a real decision. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas was ill and thought he might die. He was wealthy, with one daughter as his heir. He asked the Prophet ﷺ if he could give two-thirds of his wealth away in charity. No, he was told. Half? No. A third? A third, the Prophet said, and a third is a lot. Better to leave your heirs well off than to leave them dependent on other people. Even generosity has a middle. The question isn't only, am I giving enough? It's also, am I keeping enough for the people I'm responsible for? The firm station is where both questions get a fair answer. And it isn't a single number. It moves with your life.
screen: `ISRAF: GOING PAST THE LIMIT.` · `QATR: SQUEEZING TIGHT.` · `QAWAM: STANDING UPRIGHT BETWEEN.` · `A THIRD, AND A THIRD IS A LOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one purchase. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of something you bought this week, or are about to buy. Ask two questions. Is this past what I need, or what's right? And on the other side: am I holding back somewhere I should be giving, to myself, to my family, to someone in need? Don't scold yourself. Just look for where the firm middle would stand. The bell holds the time.
Qawam. A firm, upright station between prodigal and grudging spending, standing steady, not tipping either way. Today's word.
Your line: in between. Today, before one purchase, pause and ask whether it's past the limit, or whether you're squeezing too tight. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

500.title: Bad deeds turned to good
500.hook: for those who repent and do good, Allah changes their bad deeds to good (25:70)
500.tomorrow: Block B close: prophets and light
500.howItsDone: Muslims describe repentance, tawba, as turning back to God with regret, stopping the wrong and resolving not to return to it; teachers often quote 25:70 to show that no one is beyond turning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qawam, between the two, and your line was in between. Which purchase did you pause over? Day five hundred. That's a lot of mornings.

A ledger is supposed to be permanent. That's the whole point of one. Whatever you wrote in the red column stays in the red column, and the best you can hope for is enough in the black to outweigh it. Some people carry a version of that ledger around in their heads: a list of the worst things they've done. The portrait of the servants of the Merciful has reached its hardest verses: the serious wrongs, and what happens to someone who has done them. And the next line does something no ledger is supposed to do.
screen: `A LEDGER IS SUPPOSED TO BE PERMANENT.`

segments.voice: Verses sixty-eight and sixty-nine name grave wrongs: calling on another god, killing a soul unjustly, adultery. They say plainly that whoever does these meets a heavy penalty. Then verse seventy opens a door. Except, it says, the one who repents, and believes, and does good work. And then: "Allah will change their evil deeds to good deeds." The verb is yubaddilu, to exchange, to swap one thing for another. Not erase. Exchange. Commentators have read this in two ways. One reading is about this life. A person who turns around doesn't just stop the old habits; the energy that went into them starts going somewhere good. The one who used to lie becomes careful with the truth. The one who used to take starts to give. The bad deeds are replaced by good ones, in the living of it. The other reading goes further, and it rests on a hadith in Muslim's collection. On the Day of Judgment, a man is shown his small sins, one by one, while his great ones are held back. He braces himself. Then he's told: for each bad deed, you have a good one in its place. And suddenly the man says, wait, I did other things too, I don't see them here. And the Prophet ﷺ, telling this, laughed until his back teeth showed. Either way, the ledger isn't what it seemed. The verse ends: God is ever Forgiving, Merciful. And the verse after says whoever repents and does good has truly turned to God.
screen: `THE GRAVE WRONGS NAMED.` · `EXCEPT THE ONE WHO TURNS.` · `YUBADDILU: EXCHANGE, NOT ERASE.` · `I DON'T SEE THEM HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin again today. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one thing in your own red column, something you regret. Don't relive it. Just name it. Then ask: what's the opposite of that, the good deed that could stand in its place? If you were careless with someone, it might be care. If you took, it might be giving. Pick one small version you can do today. If you pray, you can ask for it to be turned. The bell holds the time.
Ledger. The record this lesson overturns: for the one who repents, God exchanges the bad deeds for good ones. Today's word.
Your line: turned to good. Today, do the small opposite you picked, and let it be a beginning rather than a payment. Day five hundred.

501.title: Block B close: prophets and light
501.hook: Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Musa, Yusuf, Maryam, Ayyub, Yunus, all in one arc
501.carry: they all said the same one thing
501.howItsDone: Muslims believe in all the prophets the Qur'an names, from Adam to Muhammad, as one line of messengers bringing the same core message of God's oneness, and add 'peace be upon him' after each name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ledger turned to good, and your line was turned to good. What small opposite did you do? Day five hundred one, the last day of Block B.

Seventy-two days ago, on day four hundred twenty-nine, Block B opened with Surah Yunus. Since then the path has walked through sixteen surahs, from Yunus to Al-Furqan, and they've been crowded with people. A man building a ship on dry land while his neighbors laughed. Two prophets warning two vanished peoples. A boy thrown into a well who grew up to forgive his brothers. A man who saw a fire in the desert and walked toward it. A young mother under a palm tree. A sick man who named his pain. A prophet calling out from the dark inside a whale. Different centuries, different places. And yet.
screen: `A SHIP ON DRY LAND, A BOY IN A WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's Block B in a handful of doors. Yunus and Hud: Nuh and his ark, Hud and Salih sent to 'Ad and Thamud, and the friends of God who neither fear nor grieve. Yusuf: the well, the prison, and no blame on you today. Ar-Ra'd and Ibrahim: the thunder glorifying, and a good word like a good tree. Al-Isra and Al-Kahf: the night journey, the young men in the cave, and the stranger who explained what Musa couldn't bear. Maryam and Ta-Ha: the palm tree in labor, the fire Musa walked toward, and 'ilm, increase me in knowledge. Al-Anbiya: Ayyub, Zakariyya, and rahmatan lil-'alamin. Al-Hajj, Al-Mu'minun, An-Nur, Al-Furqan: the pilgrims' call, the believers, light upon light, and the servants of the Merciful who walk gently. Now listen for the line that keeps coming back. Surah Hud tells the stories of Nuh, Hud, Salih and Shu'ayb, and each of them opens with nearly the same words to his people: worship God; you have no god but Him. Al-Anbiya says it outright: God sent no messenger before Muhammad ﷺ without revealing to him that there is no god but God, so worship Him. That's the arc of this whole block. The Qur'an doesn't present these prophets as founders of different faiths. It presents them as one long line of messengers, each sent to their own people in their own language, each saying the same one thing. Different storms, different deserts, different kings. One message. And between the stories, light: on a lamp in a niche, on a pilgrim's road, on a heart that sees.
screen: `NUH, HUD, SALIH; THE FRIENDS OF GOD.` · `YUSUF; THE CAVE; THE PALM; THE FIRE.` · `AYYUB; LIGHT UPON LIGHT.` · `ONE LINE OF MESSENGERS, ONE MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name a prophet you feel close to. Sit, and breathe. Let the faces of this block pass by slowly: Nuh, Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Yusuf, Musa, Maryam, Zakariyya, Ayyub, Yunus. Notice which one you stay with. The one in the well, maybe, or the one in the dark, or the one asking not to be left alone. Ask yourself why that one. When the bell ends, write down the name and one sentence about why. If you pray, you can send peace on them. The bell holds the time.
Rasul, a messenger: the word for every prophet from Yunus to Al-Furqan, one long line of messengers sent with the same message. Today's word.

Your line: they all said the same one thing. Tomorrow, the path steps into the Islamic year itself, its holy days and months, starting with Muharram. Today, keep your prophet's name with you. Day five hundred one.

502.title: Muharram: a new year
502.hook: the Islamic calendar begins from the Hijra, and the new year is quiet reflection
502.carry: a new year from the hijra
502.howItsDone: Many Muslims greet one another at the start of Muharram and reflect on the Hijra; there is no prescribed new year ritual, and practice varies widely between communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Block B, the word rasul, and your line was they all said the same one thing. Which prophet did you name as the one you feel close to? Day five hundred two, and a new stretch of the path.
screen: `THEY ALL SAID THE SAME ONE THING.`

segments.voice: On the first night of the Islamic new year, in many Muslim communities, there are no fireworks at midnight. No countdown. Some families exchange greetings, some mosques hold a talk, and for many people it passes quietly, like a page turning. For the next two weeks, this path steps out of the surahs and walks through the Islamic year itself: its holy days, its months, its fasts and feasts. And the first question is simple. Why does this calendar start where it does?

The Islamic calendar counts from the Hijra, the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ emigration from Mecca to Medina, in the year 622 of the common era. That's why it's called Hijri, and why dates are marked AH, after the Hijra. The choice was made years later, under the second caliph, 'Umar. Letters were arriving with months but no years, and people needed a common count. Reports say they considered the Prophet's birth, or the first revelation, and chose the Hijra instead: the moment a persecuted group became a community with a home. The year was set to begin with Muharram, which reports say was already felt as the turn of the year, after the pilgrimage season, even though the journey itself took place a little later in the year. Surah At-Tawbah says: "Lo! the number of the months with Allah is twelve months", and four of them are sacred. Muharram is one of the four. The months are lunar, each beginning with the new crescent moon, and what that does to the holy days is where these two weeks will end. A hadith in Muslim's collection calls Muharram the month of God, and says the best fast after Ramadan is in it. There is no set ritual for the new year itself. Some Muslims use it to remember the turning point the calendar counts from, and to ask where they themselves are heading. For Shia Muslims, the month also opens a season of mourning, which we'll come to in two days.
screen: `COUNTED FROM THE HIJRA, 622.` · `CHOSEN UNDER 'UMAR.` · `TWELVE MONTHS, FOUR SACRED.` · `MONTHS BY THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set one intention for the year. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think back over the last twelve months: one thing you're glad of, one thing you'd leave behind. Then choose one intention for the year ahead. Small and real, something you could still be doing next Muharram. Say it to yourself in one sentence. If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
Hijri. The Islamic calendar, counted from the Hijra, the emigration to Medina: twelve lunar months, beginning with Muharram. Today's word.
Your line: a new year from the hijra. Today, write your one intention down somewhere you'll see it again, a note on your phone or a slip in your wallet. Day five hundred two.

503.title: Ashura: the fast of Musa
503.hook: the Prophet ﷺ fasted the tenth of Muharram in thanks for Musa's rescue (Bukhari)
503.howItsDone: Many Sunni Muslims fast on the tenth of Muharram, often with the ninth or eleventh as well, as a voluntary fast of gratitude; the day is observed differently in Shia communities, as a day of mourning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hijri year, and your line was a new year from the hijra. Where did you write your intention down? Day five hundred three.

A newcomer has just arrived in a town, tired, after a dangerous journey. On one particular day, he notices that many of his new neighbors aren't eating. He asks why. And they tell him: this is the day God rescued Musa and his people from Pharaoh, and drowned Pharaoh's army, and Musa fasted on this day in thanks, so we fast too. According to Bukhari, that's roughly what happened when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina and saw the Jewish community fasting on the tenth day of the month.
screen: `A NEW TOWN, A DAY OF FASTING.`

segments.voice: The day is called 'Ashura, from 'ashara, ten. It's the tenth of Muharram. Bukhari records Ibn 'Abbas describing the scene. The Prophet asked about the fast, heard the reason, and said that Muslims too had a claim to Musa, a bond with him. So he fasted that day, and told his companions to fast it. So the Muslims in Medina joined in giving thanks for Musa's rescue, because they counted Musa as theirs too. Another report, from 'A'isha, says the Quraysh in Mecca had already fasted 'Ashura before Islam, and the Prophet had fasted it there. Then, once the fast of Ramadan was made a duty, 'Ashura became optional: whoever wished to fast it fasted, and whoever wished to leave it left it. A hadith in Muslim's collection says the fast of 'Ashura is hoped to wipe away the faults of the year before. And another, also in Muslim, says that late in his life the Prophet resolved that if he lived another year he would fast the ninth as well. He died before that year came, which is why some fast the ninth with the tenth, and some the tenth with the eleventh. So among Sunni Muslims, the tenth of Muharram is mostly a day of fasting in gratitude, rooted in an older story: the sea opening, the people crossing, the army gone. Tomorrow, the same date holds a very different memory, one that came later, and is kept with grief.
screen: `'ASHURA: THE TENTH.` · `WE HAVE A CLAIM TO MUSA TOO.` · `OPTIONAL ONCE RAMADAN CAME.` · `THE NINTH AND THE TENTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for a rescue. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of a time you were pulled out of something. An illness you recovered from, a mistake that didn't turn out as badly as it could have, a person who showed up at the right moment. Stay with that memory for a moment. If you're able, you can fast a day this week, or give up one comfort, as a thank-you. If you pray, you can say so. The bell holds the time.
'Ashura. The tenth of Muharram, which the Prophet fasted in thanks for Musa's rescue from Pharaoh. Today's word.
Your line: thanks for a rescue. Today, tell one person who once helped you out of a hole that you still remember it. Day five hundred three.

504.title: Ashura: Husayn at Karbala
504.hook: Shia Muslims mourn the martyrdom of Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, at Karbala in 680, and many Sunnis grieve him too
504.howItsDone: Shia Muslims observe the first ten days of Muharram with mourning gatherings (majalis), recitations of the Karbala story, processions and free water stands (sabil); many Sunni Muslims also remember Husayn on 'Ashura, often alongside fasting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fast of 'Ashura, and your line was thanks for a rescue. Who did you tell that you still remember? Day five hundred four, the end of the week.

In parts of Iraq, Iran, Lebanon, Pakistan, India and far beyond, on the tenth of Muharram, streets fill with people dressed in black. Some walk in long processions. Some sit in halls listening to a reciter tell a story they already know by heart, and weep anyway. And along the roads, people hand out water, free, to anyone who passes. Cups of it, jugs of it, stands built just for the day. The water is part of the story. Today, the same date as yesterday, and a different memory.

Husayn ibn 'Ali was the grandson of the Prophet ﷺ, the son of his daughter Fatima and of 'Ali. Hadith collections record the Prophet's deep love for him. In Tirmidhi, he says Husayn is from me and I am from Husayn. In the year 680, Yazid, son of Mu'awiya, had become ruler, and demanded the allegiance of the leading Muslims. Husayn refused to give it. He set out toward Kufa in Iraq, where people had written urging him to come, with his family and a small band of companions. At a place called Karbala, near the Euphrates, a much larger army surrounded them and cut them off from the river. For days, the camp went without water, children included. On the tenth of Muharram, Husayn and nearly all the men with him were killed. The women and children, among them his sister Zaynab, and his son 'Ali, who had been too ill to fight, were taken as captives to Kufa and then to Damascus. The sources tell that Zaynab spoke out boldly before the governor and before Yazid himself. For Shia Muslims, Karbala is at the heart of their faith and history. 'Ashura is a day of mourning, majalis gatherings, recitations and processions, a remembering that keeps the question alive: what does it mean to stand against injustice when it costs everything? Many Sunni Muslims grieve Husayn deeply too, and honor him as a member of the Prophet's family. They understand some of the events and their meaning differently, and mark the day differently. The grief for a grandson killed beside a river he wasn't allowed to drink from is shared widely. That's why there's water on the roads.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give water in his memory. Sit, and let the breath settle. Picture a family in the heat with no water, and a river just out of reach. Stay with that for a moment. Then think of who near you could use water today: a delivery driver, a coworker at a long shift, a stranger in the sun, a plant. Decide who you'll give it to. If you pray, you can remember Husayn and his family. The bell holds the time.
'Ashura again, the tenth of Muharram. For Shia Muslims above all, the day Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, was killed at Karbala. Today's word.

Your line: he stood for justice. This week ran from walking humbly and the firm middle, through deeds turned to good, a close, a new year, and two 'Ashuras. Today, hand someone a cup of water. Day five hundred four.
